strengths: Novel and Safety-Critical Problem: The paper identifies and formalizes a highly practical and previously unexamined vulnerability in state-of-the-art monocular depth estimation (MDE) foundation models—namely, hallucinating 3D structures from geometrically flat 2D illusions (the '3D Mirage' effect), which poses severe risks to autonomous driving and visual intelligence systems.

Comprehensive Benchmark (3D-Mirage): The authors present a high-quality, manually annotated dataset of 1,872 real-world illusion images complete with precise planar Region of Interest (ROI) masks and context-restricted crops, filling a notable gap in robust MDE evaluation.

Well-designed and Mathematically Sound Metrics: Proposing Laplacian-based metrics—specifically the Deviation Composite Score (DCS) and Confusion Composite Score (CCS)—provides a rigorous way to evaluate geometric non-planarity and contextual instability rather than relying on standard error metrics (MAE/RMSE) which are perceptually-blind to such local structural failures.

Effective Mitigation Strategy: The Grounded Self-Distillation pipeline using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) is elegant. By partitioning the objective into knowledge re-editing (HKR) and knowledge preservation (NKP), the method successfully flattens illusion-induced depth anomalies while preventing catastrophic forgetting on standard datasets (validated on NYUv2).

Extensive Analyses: The supplementary material and qualitative comparisons across multiple model scales and architectures (e.g., Depth-Anything, Depth Pro, Marigold, DepthFM) provide deep insight into how capacity and training domains (indoor vs. outdoor) impact hallucination susceptibility.
weaknesses: Reliance on Explicit ROI Annotations for Mitigation: The proposed Grounded Self-Distillation relies on manual or pre-defined planar ROI masks to enforce planarity. In a fully wild environment, a model might encounter novel illusions without such masks, making the mitigation strategy dependent on a curated training database rather than resolving the root architectural cause online.

Limited Architectural Evaluation of the Mitigation: While the paper demonstrates that the '3D Mirage' is a systemic failure across various architectures (transformers, diffusion, flow-matching), the proposed mitigation strategy is only implemented and validated on a transformer-based encoder (Depth-Anything V2 / DINOv2). It remains unclear how easily this strategy scales to diffusion-based depth models like Marigold.

Potential Over-Flattening Risk: Although the Non-hallucination Knowledge Preservation (NKP) loss limits flattening outside the ROI, there is still a potential risk of the adapted model over-generalizing this behavior and flattening real-world planar structures containing high-contrast texture (e.g., highly textured walls, decorated pavements, or road signs) even when they are not illusory. A quantitative false-positive analysis would have strengthened the evaluation.

strengths: Identifies a novel, highly practical, and safety-critical failure mode in monocular depth estimation (MDE) models (termed '3D Mirage'), where models hallucinate 3D structures from planar 2D patterns (such as street art) and exhibit severe context-dependence.
Introduces the first benchmark (3D-Mirage) specifically curated to probe this vulnerability, containing 1,872 images with manual planar ROI annotations and systematic context-restricted crops.

Proposes novel and mathematically grounded Laplacian-based metrics, the Deviation Composite Score (DCS) and Confusion Composite Score (CCS), which focus on structural and contextual consistency instead of average pixel-wise errors.

Develops an effective mitigation framework, Grounded Self-Distillation, leveraging parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) and dual loss objectives (HKR and NKP) to successfully resolve the hallucinations without causing catastrophic forgetting.

Provides extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations on a wide range of state-of-the-art architectures (e.g., Depth-Anything, ZoeDepth, Depth Pro, Marigold, and DepthFM) along with a thorough ablation study.
weaknesses: Generalizability of the mitigation is not fully explored: Since the model is fine-tuned and evaluated on the same 3D-Mirage dataset, it remains unclear how well the adaptation generalizes to unseen, out-of-distribution optical illusions.

Heavy reliance on manual annotations: The proposed Grounded Self-Distillation pipeline requires precise polygonal ROI masks of planar regions. This manual annotation bottleneck limits the scalability of the approach to larger datasets.

Mitigation is only demonstrated on a single architecture type: Although the failure mode is shown to affect diverse architectures (diffusion-based, generative, and feedforward transformer models), the mitigation strategy is only implemented and verified on the Depth-Anything V2 transformer encoder.

Non-standard evaluation for knowledge preservation: The authors evaluate the preservation of general depth-estimation capability on NYU-v2 using ordinal pairwise accuracy instead of standard MDE metrics (e.g., REL, RMSE, and delta thresholds), which makes it difficult to assess if absolute metric depth precision is fully maintained.

strengths: Identifies a highly novel, safety-critical vulnerability in modern state-of-the-art monocular depth estimation (MDE) foundation models, termed '3D Mirage' (depth hallucinations caused by 2D optical illusions like street art).

Introduces '3D-Mirage', a valuable first-of-its-kind benchmark consisting of real-world images of optical illusions, complete with precise planar ROI annotations and cropped versions to evaluate contextual stability.
Proposes sensible, localized Laplacian-based metrics (DCS and CCS) that are much better suited for evaluating structural failures in MDE than traditional average pixel-wise metrics.

Develops an effective 'Grounded Self-Distillation' framework that leverages parameter-efficient training (LoRA) to successfully mitigate hallucinations while preserving the foundational model's general depth perception accuracy (as verified on NYUv2).
weaknesses: The mitigation strategy heavily relies on the availability of precise human-annotated ROI masks during training to enforce planarity. In actual deployment, identifying these regions without prior annotation remains a challenge.

The formulation of the planarity loss (L_HKR) is tailored specifically to flat surfaces. While suitable for street art on roads/walls, the method's generalizability to non-planar hallucinatory patterns is limited.

The composite loss function described in Section 4.3 is quite complex and involves many hyperparameters (seven alpha weights), which suggests a high sensitivity to parameter tuning and potentially limits easy reproduction or adaptation to other models.
